p82: 82.  The Government stressed the need to distinguish the issue of the applicant’s ties with the child and of the risk of damage to those ties in the event of a return from the issue of a risk to the child’s fundamental interests within the meaning of Article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention. As an Australian citizen, the applicant had not faced insurmountable difficulties in the event of a return to Australia since she enjoyed all her fundamental rights there, unlike the applicants in Neulinger and Shuruk (cited above). In the present case both the mother and the child had Australian nationality, and the mother also had access to the labour market, as she had found employment since her return, and could receive social-welfare benefits. The family history bore no trace of violence or abuse of authority on T.’s part, whereas the applicant had shown a lack of cooperation and aggressiveness. Lastly, the Government drew the Court’s attention to the fact that they could not be held responsible for decisions taken by the Australian authorities (see M.R. and L.R. v. Estonia (dec.), cited above).
p83: 83.  The Finnish Government pointed out that the Hague Convention was based on the best interests of the child and that its aim was to protect the child from the harmful effects of abduction, while providing for a number of grounds on which return could be refused. They emphasised that the “Brussels II bis Regulation” applicable within the European Union, Article 11 of which further restricted the exceptions to the child’s return, reflected the view of the member States of the European Union that the effectiveness of the Hague Convention served the best interests of children and families. They also referred to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child.
p84: 84.  As regards the present case, they considered in particular that the obligation for domestic courts dealing with a request for return to carry out an “in-depth examination of the entire family situation”, as required by the Chamber in its judgment, was in contradiction with the Hague Convention, which provided that matters relating to custody and the child’s residence fell within the jurisdiction of the courts of the place of habitual residence.
p85: 85.  Furthermore, they considered that the national courts were best placed to determine the best interests of the child: the Court should not substitute itself for them but should confine itself to reviewing compliance with the requirements of Article 8. Requiring such an in-depth examination would blur the differences between return proceedings and custody proceedings, which might deprive the Hague Convention of its substance. They emphasised that the latter provided for exceptions to the return of the child in its Articles 12, 13 and 20.
p86: 86.  As regards the psychological report, to which, according to the Chamber judgment, the domestic courts had not attached sufficient importance, the Finnish Government noted that it had been produced by the mother in order to establish the existence of a grave risk in the event of return within the meaning of Article 13 of the Hague Convention. In finding them ill-founded, the appellate court had dismissed those allegations under Article 13 of the Hague Convention within the margin of appreciation available to it and in keeping with the objective pursued by the Hague Convention. For those reasons, and referring to the dissenting opinion of Judges Myjer and López Guerra annexed to the Chamber judgment, the Finnish Government were of the view that there had been no violation of Article 8 of the Convention in the present case.
p87: 87.  The Czech Government considered that the forthcoming decision of the Grand Chamber would be of considerable importance not only for the respondent State and the Convention system, but also for the functioning of the Hague Convention and for countries outside the European continent. They considered that the Hague Convention provided an appropriate procedure in view of the serious consequences of an abduction for the child and for the parent who was the victim of that situation. In order to avoid the harmful effects of abduction, speedy proceedings and a speedy return were necessary, the Hague Convention being based on the assumption that restoring the status quo that had existed prior to the abduction was the best starting-point for protecting the rights at stake. They also cited, to the same effect, the “Brussels II bis Regulation” applicable within the European Union.
